issues.legal_issue: A mining lease continued by statutory substitution after the vesting of an estate is a new lease for purposes of rules limited to modifying leases granted before a specified cutoff.
material_facts: A mining lease was granted before the cutoff and remained in force immediately before the estate vested in the State.
The land reform statute deemed the leased area to be leased by the State to the original lessee for the remainder of the lease term.
The Controller modified and terminated the lease under rules that applied to leases granted before the cutoff.
issues.conclusion: The majority held that the State-held lease was a new lease granted after the cutoff, so the Controller had no jurisdiction under the modification rules to modify it; the appeals were allowed and the modification orders were set aside. The dissent considered the lease a continuation of the existing lease and would have upheld the Controller’s authority.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 4 and 10 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, the original lessor’s interests vested in the State and the subsisting lease was deemed to be a lease by the State for the remainder of its term. The majority construed section 10 and the Mining Leases (Modification of Terms) Rules, 1956, including rule 2(c), to mean the resulting lease was a new lease outside the rules’ definition of an existing lease. No earlier case was relied on by the majority. The dissent, relying on the text of section 10 and contrasting it with section 9, viewed section 10 as continuing an existing lease with the State substituted as lessor.

predicates.appeal_from_mining_lease_modification_or: A party appealed an order modifying a mining lease under rules governing modification of lease terms.
predicates.lease_subsisted_before_vesting: The mining lease remained in force immediately before the estate containing the leased land vested in the State.
predicates.state_was_deemed_lessor_after_vesting: After vesting, the State was deemed to lease the land to the former lessee for the balance of the original lease term.
predicates.modification_rules_limited_to_pre_cutoff: The modification rules applied to leases granted before a specified cutoff date.

issues.definition: When a mining lease subsists before vesting, the State becomes its deemed lessor, and the modification rules cover only earlier grants, the Controller lacks authority to modify that State-held lease.

issues.legal_issue: A sublease dependent on a head lease that becomes a new State lease after vesting is likewise outside modification rules limited to leases granted before a specified cutoff.
material_facts: The head lease subsisted immediately before the estate vested and was deemed to be a lease by the State to the head lessee.
Subleases had been granted under the head lease before vesting.
The Controller also modified and terminated the subleases under the same rules used to modify the head lease.
issues.conclusion: The majority held that the subleases were also deemed to be new leases and could not be modified under the rules; the modification orders were set aside. The dissent considered the subleases continued with the head lease and could be modified.
issues.legal_principle: The majority reasoned that the original lessor’s rights under the head lease ceased upon vesting and that the head lessee held a new lease from the State; consequently, the subleases were deemed new leases derived from that new lease. Section 10 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, and rule 2(c) of the Mining Leases (Modification of Terms) Rules, 1956, informed the majority’s conclusion. The dissent relied on section 10’s continuation of the existing lease and reasoned that the sublease continued with it.

rule.if: appeal_from_sublease_modification_order and head_lease_subsisted_before_vesting and head_lease_became_new_state_lease and modification_rules_limited_to_pre_cutoff_grants

predicates.appeal_from_sublease_modification_order: A party appealed an order modifying a sublease under rules governing mining lease terms.
predicates.head_lease_subsisted_before_vesting: The head lease remained in force immediately before the estate containing the leased land vested in the State.
predicates.head_lease_became_new_state_lease: After vesting, the head lessee was deemed to hold a lease from the State for the balance of the original term.
predicates.modification_rules_limited_to_pre_cutoff: The modification rules applied to leases granted before a specified cutoff date.

issues.definition: When a head lease subsisted before vesting, became a new State lease, and the modification rules covered only earlier grants, the Controller lacks authority to modify its subleases.

issues.legal_issue: A law authorizing premature termination of a lease for extracting minerals is protected from constitutional challenge on specified individual-rights grounds when mineral extraction falls within the constitutional protection for winning minerals.
material_facts: The appellant challenged the 1957 mining statute on the ground that it permitted premature termination of a mineral lease without compensation.
The lease concerned the extraction of minerals from a mine.
issues.conclusion: The dissent held that extracting a mineral falls within the constitutional expression concerning winning minerals and that a law providing for premature termination of such a lease was protected from challenge under Articles 14, 19, and 31. The majority did not decide this contention.
issues.legal_principle: The dissent applied Article 31A(1)(e) of the Constitution and section 3(d) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, giving “winning” its popular sense of getting or extracting a mineral. It considered Lewis v. Fothergill and Lord Rokeby’s case but declined to adopt a narrower meaning. The majority left the issue undecided.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_mineral_leas: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law governing termination of mineral leases.
predicates.law_authorized_premature_termination: The challenged law authorized termination of a mineral lease before its stated expiry.
predicates.lease_concerned_mineral_extraction: The lease concerned obtaining or extracting minerals from a mine.

issues.definition: When a challenged law authorizes early termination of a lease for extracting minerals, the dissent’s rule treats the law as protected from the specified individual-rights challenge.

issues.legal_issue: Rules made under a repealed mining statute and continued by a replacement statute are valid under the replacement statute when they conform to it.
material_facts: The 1956 rules were made under the 1948 mining statute and did not provide compensation for some reductions in lease terms.
The 1957 statute repealed the 1948 statute and deemed rules made or purportedly made under the earlier statute to have been made under the replacement statute.
The dissent found the 1956 rules to conform to the 1957 statute.
issues.conclusion: The dissent held that the 1956 rules were valid under the 1957 statute despite their possible original invalidity for failing to provide compensation under the earlier statute. The majority did not decide the issue.
issues.legal_principle: The dissent applied section 29 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, which deemed the earlier rules to have been made under the 1957 Act, and assessed their validity by reference to that Act. It also addressed section 7(2)(b) of the 1948 Act and referred to Bharat Kala Mandir v. Municipal Committee, Dhamangaon, in considering whether the rules purported to have been made under the earlier Act.

rule.if: challenge_to_continued_mining_rules and rules_made_under_repealed_mining_law and replacement_law_deemed_rules_reenacted and rules_conformed_to_replacement_law

predicates.challenge_to_continued_mining_rules: A party challenged the validity of mining rules continued after replacement of the statute under which they were made.
predicates.rules_made_under_repealed_mining_law: The rules were made or purportedly made under a mining statute that was later repealed.
predicates.replacement_law_deemed_rules_reenacted: The replacement statute treated the earlier rules as having been made under the replacement statute.
predicates.rules_conformed_to_replacement_law: The rules’ requirements were consistent with the replacement statute.

issues.definition: When earlier mining rules are deemed made under a replacement law and conform to it, the dissent’s rule treats them as valid under that law.

issues.legal_issue: The maximum permitted term for an existing mining lease is measured from the lease’s commencement, not from the commencement of the replacement statute.
material_facts: The dissent treated the leases as existing mining leases subject to modification under the 1956 rules.
The minerals were not among the stated exceptions to the maximum term.
The leases had run for longer than the maximum term by the time the Controller made the termination orders.
issues.conclusion: The dissent held that the term was to be measured from the commencement of each lease, not from commencement of the 1957 statute, and upheld termination because the permitted term had already elapsed. The majority did not decide this issue.
issues.legal_principle: The dissent applied section 8 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, rule 40 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949, and sections 16 and 8 of the 1957 Act together with rules 4 and 6 of the Mining Leases (Modification of Terms) Rules, 1956. It reasoned that modification had to bring an existing lease into conformity with the permitted term, calculated from the commencement of that lease.

predicates.appeal_from_mining_lease_termination_ord: A party appealed an order terminating a mining lease after its terms were modified.
predicates.lease_was_subject_to_maximum_term: The lease concerned minerals subject to a maximum permitted lease term.
predicates.lease_exceeded_permitted_duration_from_c: The lease had continued beyond the permitted duration measured from the start of the lease.

issues.definition: When a lease is subject to a maximum term and has exceeded that term from its commencement, the dissent’s rule allows termination for exceeding the permitted duration.

issues.legal_issue: An irregular failure to give notice before modifying a sublease does not require reversal when the properly terminated head lease has already brought the sublease to an end.
material_facts: The Controller properly gave notice concerning the head lease and terminated it under one order.
The Controller gave no notice to the relevant lessees before issuing separate orders modifying the subleases.
The dissent considered that termination of the head lease automatically ended the subleases.
issues.conclusion: The dissent held that the separate sublease orders were irregular for lack of notice but saw no reason to reverse them because the properly terminated head lease had already ended the subleases. The majority set aside the modification orders for lack of authority and did not adopt this reasoning.
issues.legal_principle: The dissent applied the notice requirements in rules 4 and 6 of the Mining Leases (Modification of Terms) Rules, 1956, and reasoned that the subleases automatically ended when the head lease was properly terminated. The majority’s disposition rested instead on its conclusion that the Controller lacked jurisdiction to modify the leases.

rule.if: appeal_from_sublease_modification_order and notice_was_not_given_for_sublease_modification and head_lease_was_validly_terminated and sublease_ended_with_head_lease

predicates.appeal_from_sublease_modification_order: A party appealed an order modifying a mining sublease.
predicates.notice_was_not_given_for_sublease_modifi: The decision-maker issued the sublease modification order without giving the affected lessees the required notice.
predicates.head_lease_was_validly_terminated: The head lease was terminated by an order made after the required notice was given.
predicates.sublease_ended_with_head_lease: The sublease ended automatically when the head lease ended.

issues.definition: When notice was omitted for a sublease order but the head lease was validly terminated and the sublease ended with it, the dissent’s rule does not require reversal for the notice irregularity.
